The Battle of Crécy. On the twenty-sixth of August, thirteen forty-six, near the village of Crécy in Picardy, Edward III of England won a victory that would reshape medieval warfare itself. His force of ten thousand faced a French army of forty thousand or more—a profound numerical disadvantage that should have meant destruction. Instead, the English won decisively, and the longbow was the reason.

The French cavalry charged repeatedly against English positions, each time broken by arrows fired at a rate and penetrating power that their own crossbowmen and traditional medieval arms could not match. The devastation was immense. French nobles and thousands of soldiers fell, including many of the kingdom's finest knights. The losses weakened France's power so severely that it encouraged further English territorial expansion in France during the Hundred Years' War.

Edward's son, known as the Black Prince, fought prominently in the battle and became a celebrated military commander across all of Europe. The victory at Crécy demonstrated something fundamental about the future of warfare. Disciplined infantry armed with ranged weapons could overcome the feudal cavalry charge—the military organisation that had dominated medieval Europe for centuries. This shift would eventually reshape how all armies fought. The dominance of the longbow meant that medieval feudalism itself was becoming obsolete, though few recognised it at the time. Crécy was not just a victory; it was a revolution announced on a muddy French field.
